implementation_notes: Swift has no rate limiter in the standard library, so the pattern is hand-written; Swift concurrency supplies the pieces: an actor serializes access to the token state without an explicit lock, and ContinuousClock is the monotonic clock Apple documents with sleep(for:)/sleep(until:) for suspending a task. A non-blocking acquire() returns false and lets the caller answer 429 or back-pressure; a pacing call awaits clock.sleep(until:) for the deficit. Use the actor form for async server or client code; the GCD timer variant remains for callback-based codebases.
pitfalls: Actors serialize but do not throttle: an actor without a rate decision merely queues work, so the limit must be explicit in its state.
Date()/system time jumps under NTP; ContinuousClock is the documented monotonic basis for interval accounting.
Actor reentrancy: any await inside the method lets other messages interleave, so state must be updated before suspension points.
Task.sleep is cancellable and throws; ignoring cancellation in a pacing loop leaves pacing work running after the task is cancelled.

variants.name: DispatchSourceTimer cadence draining a queue
variants.idiom_name: DispatchSourceTimer repeating cadence draining a work queue
variants.implementation_notes: For callback-era code without async/await, the limiter is a repeating DispatchSourceTimer: makeTimerSource(queue:) plus schedule(deadline:repeating:leeway:) invokes a handler at a fixed cadence, and the handler admits at most a fixed amount of work per tick - a leaky-bucket style pacing that needs no per-request clock math. Apple documents leeway as the window in which the system may coalesce the timer, so the cadence is approximate by design; the handler runs on the timer's queue and must stay cheap.
pitfalls: The timer retains its event handler and keeps firing until cancel(); forgetting it leaks the source and its queued work.
leeway and timer coalescing make the effective rate approximate - a hard quota must not rely on the nominal cadence alone.
Batch semantics differ from per-request limits: bursts of up to batch size appear at each tick, so smooth spacing requires a smaller batch.
